scenes.title: Route events with EventBridge rules
scenes.narration: The architecture begins with an AWS service or a custom application producing an event. Events enter an EventBridge event bus, and rules use patterns against source, detail type and detail fields to decide which events match. One event may be routed to multiple targets, such as Lambda for processing, Step Functions for orchestration, or SQS for durable asynchronous handling. Explain that target IAM permissions and service resource policies still matter: successfully matching an event pattern does not automatically authorize target invocation. The source examples illustrate S3 object creation and application PutEvents calls. For a GenAI ingestion system, a rule might react to a newly uploaded document and start a controlled preprocessing pipeline. Discuss target retries, dead-letter queues, at-least-once delivery, duplicate-event handling, and monitoring as separate reliability concerns. Be cautious when using CLI examples as illustrative scaffolding: actual S3 event payloads and permissions depend on configured event delivery.  Follow the diagram from producer to target and identify where each authorization, transformation and recovery decision is enforced. Prefer service-specific guarantees to generic assumptions, and check current AWS syntax before using any illustrative code.

scenes.title: Make EventBridge delivery reliable
scenes.narration: This slide shows cross-account event ingestion into a custom EventBridge bus. A producer in a source AWS account sends an event only if the destination event bus resource policy permits the required action, with conditions that restrict the allowed principal and context. On the receiving side, a rule matches the event and routes it to either a Step Functions workflow or an SQS processing queue, according to configured targets. The reliability components are distinct: rule target retry behavior handles temporary delivery failures, a dead-letter queue captures specified unsuccessful deliveries after retry exhaustion, and an archive retains qualifying bus events for later replay. Archive replay is not the same as retrying a failed target invocation. For production systems, verify resource-policy ARNs, IAM permissions, target roles, retention periods and the actual retry policy. Make targets idempotent because delivery may be repeated. Use CloudWatch metrics and DLQ monitoring to investigate rather than assuming every published event was processed successfully.  Follow the diagram from producer to target and identify where each authorization, transformation and recovery decision is enforced. scenes.title: Schedule work with EventBridge Scheduler
scenes.narration: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler creates one-time or recurring tasks without maintaining a server that checks the clock. A schedule expression can specify a fixed date or use rate and cron syntax, with explicit time zone support for local business hours. When a schedule fires, Scheduler assumes an IAM execution role authorized to invoke its target, such as a Lambda function or Step Functions state machine. It can use a configurable flexible time window to distribute workload across a period and retry transient target-delivery failures within configured policies. A dead-letter queue can capture invocations that fail after the allowed attempts or event age. In an AI application, a daily summarization job could launch a state machine that retrieves authorized datasets and updates results. The sample JSON and CLI blocks on the slide are illustrative: check each current API parameter, target ARN, execution role and cron expression before copying them. Retries mean the target should use idempotency keys or inspect existing job state to prevent duplicate billing or writes. scenes.title: Connect sources and targets with EventBridge Pipes
scenes.narration: EventBridge Pipes connects a supported event source, such as an SQS queue, to a target without requiring a custom polling service. The main diagram separates four responsibilities. First, optional filtering discards events that do not match the business pattern. Second, optional input transformation reshapes the source payload for downstream consumers. Third, optional enrichment can call a supported service, such as Lambda or a workflow, to add business context. Fourth, the processed event reaches a target such as an EventBridge bus, Lambda or another supported destination. Unlike an EventBridge rule, a pipe reads directly from a specific supported source and may control batching and source-specific behavior. When using SQS, visibility timeouts, retries, batch failures and dead-letter strategies require careful design. The example configuration and CLI snippets are conceptual and must be validated for the deployed source and target. In GenAI architectures, Pipes can transform or enrich events before a knowledge-base ingestion or processing workflow begins.  Follow the diagram from producer to target and identify where each authorization, transformation and recovery decision is enforced.
